title: 10 Takeaways from Sold a Story
author: Michael J. Petrilli
summary: Mike Petrilli of the Fordham Institute rounds up the reaction to season two of Sold a Story, Emily Hanford's podcast on Direct Instruction and Project Follow Through, and distils ten themes. He moves from meta points (earlier reformers, high expectations, the claim that schools and teaching matter) to instructional ones: precise rather than improvised teaching, high-quality instructional materials, and empirical testing of every program. Drawing on Michael Pershan and Kelsey Piper, he argues that most teachers are not ideologically opposed to direct instruction but are pulled toward a mediocre default, which makes the problem technical and solvable with better materials. He lays out the unresolved debates over which outcomes matter, whether poor children should get more structured schooling, and whether capital-D Direct Instruction suits every grade and subject, quoting Linda Diamond's reply to Natalie Wexler. The newsletter then turns to policy: the federal scholarship tax credit, state-led reform in Alabama, Chad Aldeman's call for more go energy, governance reform in New York and California, and a headline link list. Throughout it is a curated digest with Petrilli's own editorial framing, archived as a roundup.
points: Petrilli, following Pershan and Piper, argues teachers are drawn to a mediocre default rather than opposed to direct instruction, which turns the problem into a technical one solvable with high-quality instructional materials.
He reads Engelmann's scripts as accumulated learning from trial and error, meant to spare teachers mistakes already made and fixed, not as a way to teacher-proof the classroom.
The Project Follow Through lesson is that every program should be tested empirically for outcomes, yet the field today mostly checks alignment to standards rather than results.
The unresolved tradeoff is whether structured, even scripted, schooling is right for poor children, and Petrilli's answer is that high expectations about academic potential cannot be waived.
Whether Direct Instruction travels beyond early reading is contested, with Mead and Wexler doubting it and Diamond answering that the method is separate from the content it can carry.
quotes: We should all keep in mind: We Gen-Xers, Millennials, and Gen-Zers weren’t the first ones to try to fix our school system. There’s a lineage from those Project Follow Through folks, to the era of the New American Schools, to the early charter school pioneers and TFA, to Doug Lemov and Teach Like a Champion, and through to today.
But while those things count, great schools can move the needle and great teaching can help kids learn a lot more than they otherwise would.

So I say this with no disrespect for my profession, but teachers in this country are not ideologically opposed to direct instruction. Instead we’re actively drawn to the mediocre default; it has gravity.

That’s what DI was all those years ago: a tested, meticulously designed program that broke down “instructional moves” into discrete parts. It’s nuts to ask teachers to figure out these moves (or the entire curriculum) on their own, as Robert always argues.

But the lesson still applies: We should be willing to put our favorite programs and curricula to the test and find out if they work to boost academic achievement and other important outcomes. And we should be honest that we’re not doing much of this today, relying instead on analyses of how well various instructional materials match academic standards.
At some point, either we believe that it matters whether kids achieve their full academic potential or we don’t. See points two and three!

It’s not that Zig Engelmann didn’t trust teachers or thought they weren’t smart. It’s that he was impatient and thought it was crazy for teachers to make the same mistakes that he (and others on his team) had already made and fixed. This is how progress is made in any field of human endeavor: through trial, error, and improvement.
In my view, K–12 education has been riddled with too much “stop energy” and not enough “go energy,” in the words of Jennifer Pahlka.
